scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a recommendation response that defends independent judgment while insisting officials respect the public will; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Elected leaders in a democracy are chosen to serve the people, yet also for their judgment.
Some people recommend that government officials should rely on their own judgment rather than unquestioningly carry out the will of the people they serve.
I agree that officials must use their own judgment, but I believe they cannot simply ignore the will of the people in a democracy.
First, officials often need to follow their own judgment rather than public opinion alone.
Ordinary citizens cannot study every issue in detail, while officials have access to experts and information.
For example, a sudden public panic might demand a harmful policy that a wiser leader knows would do real damage.
This shows that sound judgment can protect a society from its own short-term fears and mistakes.
Leaders are also sometimes required to defend unpopular minorities whom the majority would happily ignore.
A leader who only follows opinion polls may abandon principle whenever the public mood shifts.
In this sense, independent judgment is an essential part of responsible leadership.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why the public will matters

sentences.text: Second, however, officials cannot simply ignore the will of the people they were chosen to serve.
In a democracy, leaders gain their authority from the citizens and are meant to represent them.
Consider an official who repeatedly overrules the clear wishes of the public, convinced that he always knows best.
Such behaviour can quickly slide into arrogance and into rule that no longer answers to anyone.
Officials who lose touch with the people they serve also lose the trust that makes government work.
The will of the people, expressed through votes and debate, is a vital check on those in power.
Good officials, then, must weigh their own judgment against the voice of the public.
In conclusion, leaders should certainly use their own judgment, especially to resist panic and protect the weak.
But ignoring the will of the people would betray the very purpose of democratic government.
The wisest officials blend independent judgment with genuine respect for those they serve.
